lesson.title: Building Bigger Continuous Functions: Continuity of Composites
lesson.summary: Composing two continuous functions produces another continuous function wherever the composition is actually defined, which is what lets complicated expressions like square roots of polynomials be declared continuous instantly.
lesson.body:
Composite functions are built by feeding the output of one function into another, written (f of g)(x) = f(g(x)). The composite continuity theorem says that if g is continuous at c, and f is continuous at g(c), then the composite f of g is continuous at c as well. More broadly, if g is continuous on its domain and f is continuous on its domain, the composite f of g is continuous at every x where the composition is actually defined, meaning every x in the domain of g for which g(x) also lands inside the domain of f. This theorem is what allows complicated formulas to be recognized as continuous instantly, by breaking them apart into simpler continuous pieces rather than checking the full limit definition from scratch.

The reasoning behind the theorem is intuitive: continuity of g at c means g(x) can be made as close as desired to g(c) by keeping x close enough to c. Continuity of f at g(c) then means f(g(x)) can be made as close as desired to f(g(c)) by keeping g(x) close enough to g(c). Chaining those two guarantees together, keeping x close to c forces g(x) close to g(c), which in turn forces f(g(x)) close to f(g(c)), which is exactly the statement that f of g is continuous at c.

Worked example: let h(x) = sqrt(x^2 - 4), and consider the point c = 3. Write h as a composite, h = f of g, where g(x) = x^2 - 4 and f(u) = sqrt(u). The inner function g is a polynomial, so it is continuous everywhere, including at c = 3, where g(3) = 9 - 4 = 5. The outer function f is continuous on its domain [0, infinity), which includes u = 5. Since g is continuous at 3 and f is continuous at g(3) = 5, the composite continuity theorem guarantees h is continuous at x = 3. As a direct check, lim(x to 3) sqrt(x^2 - 4) = sqrt(lim(x to 3) (x^2 - 4)) = sqrt(9 - 4) = sqrt(5), and h(3) = sqrt(9 - 4) = sqrt(5) as well, so the limit matches the function value exactly, confirming continuity directly.

The domain restriction in the theorem matters just as much as the continuity itself. The full domain where h(x) = sqrt(x^2 - 4) is even defined, let alone continuous, is the set of x where x^2 - 4 >= 0, meaning x <= -2 or x >= 2, since the inner expression has to land inside the domain of the square root function before the outer function can act on it at all. Outside that set, for instance at x = 0, h is not defined, so continuity of the composite is never even a question there. The theorem only makes a promise at points where the composition is defined in the first place.

This same idea explains the essential discontinuity example from earlier, sin(1/x) at x = 0, from the composite point of view. Here the outer function sin is continuous everywhere, and the inner function 1/x is continuous everywhere except at x = 0. The composite continuity theorem only guarantees continuity of sin(1/x) at points where 1/x is itself continuous, which is every x except 0, so the theorem correctly says nothing about x = 0 and does not contradict the fact that sin(1/x) is discontinuous, in the essential sense, exactly there. Composing continuous functions is a powerful shortcut, but it is only as strong as the domains of the pieces being combined.
